concepts.name: Disinvestment vs. Privatisation: Definitional Distinction
key_dimensions: Disinvestment as partial sale of government equity vs. privatisation as transfer of management control
Strategic disinvestment (>51% stake transfer) as the threshold that constitutes privatisation
Minority disinvestment retaining government majority — why it does NOT constitute privatisation
UPSC trap: Conflating all disinvestment with privatisation; understanding that privatisation is a subset

concepts.name: Strategic Disinvestment: Definition, Criteria, and Process
key_dimensions: NITI Aayog's role in identifying CPSEs for strategic disinvestment vs. Department of Investment and Public Asset Management (DIPAM) executing the process
Core vs. non-core sector classification and its bearing on disinvestment eligibility
Transaction advisors, asset monetisation, and bidding process under strategic disinvestment
Examples: Air India (completed), BPCL (stalled), Pawan Hans — distinguishing completed from failed cases

concepts.name: DIPAM: Mandate, Functions, and Institutional Role
key_dimensions: DIPAM vs. erstwhile Department of Disinvestment — evolution and expanded mandate
DIPAM's role in managing government's investment in CPSEs, ETFs, and OFS mechanisms
DIPAM vs. NITI Aayog: Who recommends vs. who executes disinvestment
UPSC trap: Confusing DIPAM (under Ministry of Finance) with other regulatory bodies like SEBI in the disinvestment process

concepts.name: Disinvestment Proceeds: Accounting, Utilisation, and Fiscal Implications
key_dimensions: National Investment Fund (NIF): Creation, modification in 2013, and current rules for utilisation of disinvestment proceeds
Disinvestment receipts classified as 'capital receipts' — implications for fiscal deficit calculation
Whether disinvestment reduces fiscal deficit: Accounting treatment and the 'asset swap' critique
UPSC trap: Disinvestment proceeds reducing fiscal deficit on paper but not improving fiscal health structurally

concepts.name: National Investment Fund (NIF): Structure and Evolution
key_dimensions: Original NIF (2005): Non-lapsable fund, proceeds invested and only returns used for social/capital spending
2013 amendment: Full proceeds directly routed to Consolidated Fund of India for budget use — dilution of ring-fencing
Current status: NIF largely a notional account; proceeds merged with general revenues
Policy critique: Loss of dedicated capital expenditure financing vs. flexibility argument

concepts.name: Methods of Disinvestment: OFS, IPO, ETF, and Strategic Sale
key_dimensions: Offer for Sale (OFS) through stock exchange: Speed, transparency, retail investor reservation (10%)
CPSE ETF and Bharat-22 ETF: Basket disinvestment, advantages of price discovery and retail participation
Initial Public Offering (IPO) vs. Follow-on Public Offer (FPO) for unlisted vs. already listed CPSEs
UPSC trap: CPSE ETF managed by Nippon AMC vs. Bharat-22 ETF managed by ICICI Prudential AMC — distinguishing the two

concepts.name: CPSE ETF and Bharat-22 ETF: Composition and Objectives
key_dimensions: CPSE ETF: 12 CPSEs, tracks Nifty CPSE Index; sectors dominated by energy and natural resources
Bharat-22 ETF: 22 stocks including CPSEs, PSBs, and government holdings in private firms (e.g., Axis Bank via SUUTI)
Objective: Retail participation in disinvestment, price discovery, avoiding market flooding
SUUTI (Specified Undertaking of UTI) holdings within Bharat-22 — a frequently tested nuance

concepts.name: Disinvestment Targets vs. Achievements: Fiscal Reality
key_dimensions: Consistent shortfall in disinvestment targets — reasons: market conditions, political opposition, litigation
Implications of shortfall: Compensatory borrowing, compression of capital expenditure, or creative accounting
Pattern: Government relying on LIC IPO, Coal India OFS as large single-transaction receipts
UPSC angle: Whether ambitious disinvestment targets are credible fiscal policy or 'fiscal illusion'

concepts.name: Rationale for Disinvestment and Privatisation: Economic Arguments
key_dimensions: Reducing fiscal burden of loss-making CPSEs (recurrent bailouts, sovereign guarantees)
Unlocking value: Argument that government is a poor owner of commercial enterprises
Revenue mobilisation for capital expenditure without inflationary money creation
Counter-arguments: Natural monopoly justification, strategic sector control, employment concerns

concepts.name: New Public Sector Enterprise Policy (2021): Categorisation of Sectors
key_dimensions: Strategic sectors: Maximum 4 PSEs; remaining to be privatised or merged — four strategic sectors identified
Non-strategic sectors: Full privatisation or closure — government has no business being in business
Rationale: Minimising government footprint in commercial activity while retaining presence in strategic areas
UPSC trap: Identifying which sectors fall under 'strategic' (atomic energy, space, defence, certain financial services) vs. non-strategic

concepts.name: Air India Privatisation: Case Study in Strategic Disinvestment
key_dimensions: Failed disinvestment attempt (2018) vs. successful Tata Sons acquisition (2022) — what changed
Employee liabilities, debt transfer structure (SPV for debt), and land/non-core asset handling
Role of DIPAM, transaction advisors, and inter-ministerial group in the process
Policy lesson: First privatisation of a loss-making Maharatna-equivalent airline; precedent for future strategic sales

concepts.name: Privatisation of Public Sector Banks (PSBs): Policy Debate
key_dimensions: Budget 2021-22 announcement: Privatisation of 2 PSBs beyond IDBI Bank — current status and challenges
Constitutional and legal hurdles: Bank Nationalisation Acts, requirement of Parliamentary amendment
IDBI Bank privatisation: LIC's role as promoter, RBI's 'fit and proper' criteria for acquirer
UPSC trap: Distinction between privatising a PSB (transfer of majority stake) vs. disinvesting (partial stake sale while government retains control)

concepts.name: Asset Monetisation vs. Disinvestment: Conceptual Distinction
key_dimensions: Asset monetisation: Leasing/transferring operational rights of existing public assets without selling ownership
National Monetisation Pipeline (NMP): ₹6 lakh crore target over 4 years (2021-25), sectors covered
Disinvestment transfers ownership (equity); monetisation retains ownership but transfers revenue rights — key distinction
UPSC trap: Treating NMP proceeds as disinvestment receipts — they are separate; NMP proceeds are capital receipts but not equity disinvestment

concepts.name: National Monetisation Pipeline (NMP): Structure and Instruments
key_dimensions: Instruments: Toll-Operate-Transfer (TOT), InvIT, REIT, OM (Operate-Maintain-Transfer), long-term lease
Sectors: Roads (NHAI), Railways, Power (PGCIL), Gas pipelines (GAIL), Telecom (BSNL towers)
Core principle: 'Brownfield asset' monetisation — already operational, de-risked assets for private operators
Criticism: Undervaluation risk, long-term revenue loss to government, regulatory capture

concepts.name: Role of NITI Aayog in Disinvestment: Recommendation vs. Execution
key_dimensions: NITI Aayog identifies CPSEs for strategic disinvestment and submits recommendations to Core Group of Secretaries on Disinvestment (CGD)
CGD: Chaired by Cabinet Secretary — inter-ministerial coordination body; distinct from CCEA which gives final approval
NITI Aayog has no executive authority — only advisory; DIPAM executes; CCEA approves
UPSC trap: Conflating NITI Aayog's recommendatory role with DIPAM's executive role or CCEA's approval authority

concepts.name: SEBI Regulations and Disinvestment: Mandatory Open Offer and Exemptions
key_dimensions: SEBI Takeover Code (SAST Regulations 2011): Acquisition of >25% triggers mandatory open offer to public shareholders
Government disinvestment to strategic buyer triggers open offer — cost implications for acquirer
SEBI exemptions: Government-to-government transfers, reorganisation of government holdings may be exempt
UPSC angle: Why SEBI open offer requirement has been a deterrent in strategic disinvestment deals (e.g., BPCL)

concepts.name: Workers and Employee Concerns in Disinvestment: Legal and Policy Dimensions
key_dimensions: Industrial Disputes Act provisions: Retrenchment, VRS (Voluntary Retirement Scheme), and employee protection clauses in sale agreements
Trade union opposition and strikes as a political economy constraint on disinvestment
Government policy: VRS packages, service condition protection clauses in strategic sale agreements (e.g., Air India — 1-year no-retrenchment clause)
Constitutional angle: Article 43A (worker participation in management) and whether privatisation violates Directive Principles

concepts.name: Disinvestment and Market Impact: Overhang Effect
key_dimensions: Share price depression when large government stake sale is announced — 'overhang effect'
OFS and ETF mechanisms designed to mitigate overhang by spreading sale over time or using basket approach
Lock-in provisions and tranched sales to prevent market disruption
UPSC angle: Why market timing matters for disinvestment receipts and how poor timing leads to target shortfalls

concepts.name: Cross-Subsidisation and Universal Service Obligations Post-Privatisation
key_dimensions: CPSEs like BSNL, Air India, Coal India serve remote/uneconomic areas — private firms may abandon these routes
Universal Service Obligation Fund (USOF) in telecom: Mechanism to fund universal access after privatisation
Regulatory frameworks required to ensure private firms fulfil public service mandates
Policy dilemma: Privatisation efficiency gains vs. equity/access concerns in sectors with natural monopoly or public good characteristics

concepts.name: Disinvestment and Constitutional Provisions: Parliamentary Oversight
key_dimensions: No explicit constitutional bar on privatisation; Parliament's approval required only when enabling Acts need amendment (e.g., bank nationalisation acts)
CCEA (Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs) as the apex approval body — executive decision, not legislative
CAG audit of disinvestment transactions: Scope, findings on undervaluation, and accountability
UPSC trap: Whether Parliament must approve each disinvestment — answer is NO for equity sales, but YES if the parent statute requires amendment
